stem: An interviewer shows a Figma mock of a product card: image, title, price, an **Add to cart** button, a heart icon that marks the product as wishlisted, and a chevron that expands a details section. The wishlist must stay in sync with the wishlist page and the header badge. How should you split the data for `<ProductCard>`?

options.text: Pass `product` and `isWishlisted` as props, take `onAddToCart` and `onToggleWishlist` callbacks, and keep `isExpanded` as local state
options.why: Data owned elsewhere arrives as props, changes go up through callbacks, and the UI-only toggle that nobody else needs stays inside the card.

options.text: Copy `product` into `useState` on mount, and keep `isWishlisted` and `isExpanded` as local state so the card is self-contained
options.why: The copied product goes stale when the parent passes new data, and a wishlist flag held inside the card cannot update the header badge or the wishlist page.

options.text: Pass `isExpanded` and `onToggleExpand` from the parent as well, so the parent controls every piece of state the card shows
options.why: Nothing outside the card needs the expanded flag. Lifting it adds props and re-renders the whole list on each toggle without any benefit.

options.text: Read the product, cart and wishlist from a global store inside the card, so it takes no props at all and every page only renders `<ProductCard />`
options.why: A card that takes no props cannot say which product it shows, and wiring a presentational card to global state makes it hard to reuse and test.

explanation: This is the "Thinking in React" exercise in interview form. For each value, ask who owns it and who else needs it. The product data and the wishlist flag are owned higher up (a list response, a wishlist store), so they come in as props and changes go out through callbacks. A value that only this card uses and that changes with interaction (the expanded section) is local state. Interviewers want to hear this reasoning, not just a working card.

stem: You are turning a Figma card into a `<ProductCard>` that the listing page, the cart page and the wishlist page all use. Each page shows different action buttons under the price. Which two design choices are sound? (Choose two.)

options.text: Accept the buttons as an `actions` (or `children`) prop, so each page passes the buttons it needs
options.why: Composition keeps the card ignorant of page-specific variants; a new page needs no change to the card.

options.text: Read `product.price` straight from props during render instead of copying it into state with `useState(product.price)`
options.why: `useState` only uses its argument on the first render, so a copied price would not update when the parent passes a new product.

options.text: Add one boolean per page (`isCart`, `isWishlist`, `isListing`) and branch inside the card to pick the buttons
options.why: Every new page or variant adds another flag and more branches, and combinations of flags become ambiguous.

options.text: Have each card fetch its own product by id in an effect, so pages only pass `productId`
options.why: The page already has the data from one list request; per-card fetching turns a 50-item list into 50 requests and 50 loading states.

options.text: Keep the hover highlight in page-level state so the page always knows which card is hovered
options.why: Nothing else needs it; CSS `:hover` handles it without state, and page-level state re-renders every card on each mouse move.

explanation: Reusable components take data in through props and let callers fill the variable parts through `children` or slot props. Two common mistakes come up when candidates design a card from a mock: mirroring props into state (the copy goes stale) and piling up boolean variant props. The interviewer is checking whether your component API will survive the third and fourth page that uses it.

stem:
A client-side pagination component shows 10 of 23 loaded items per page. `page` is 1-based and the user is on page 3. Which code computes the page count and the visible rows correctly?

```js
const pageSize = 10; // items.length === 23, page === 3
```

options.text: `Math.ceil(items.length / pageSize)` and `items.slice((page - 1) * pageSize, page * pageSize)`
options.why: That gives 3 pages, and page 3 is `slice(20, 30)`, which returns the last three items (21 to 23).

options.text: `Math.floor(items.length / pageSize)` and `items.slice((page - 1) * pageSize, page * pageSize)`
options.why: `Math.floor(23 / 10)` is 2, so the last three items have no page at all.

options.text: `Math.ceil(items.length / pageSize)` and `items.slice((page - 1) * pageSize, pageSize)`
options.why: The second argument of `slice` is an end index, not a count. `slice(20, 10)` returns an empty array.

options.text: `Math.ceil(items.length / pageSize)` and `items.splice((page - 1) * pageSize, pageSize)`
options.why: `splice` removes the items from the array it is called on, which mutates state and makes the next render lose rows.

explanation: Page count is `Math.ceil(total / pageSize)`, so a partial last page still counts. The rows for a 1-based page are `slice(start, end)` with `start = (page - 1) * pageSize` and `end = start + pageSize`. `slice` clamps the end to the array length and does not mutate. Interviewers often follow up with server-side pagination, where the same maths becomes `offset` and `limit` parameters.

options.why: The set holds 1, 10, 3, 4 and 5. Sorted, there is a gap between 1 and 3 and another between 5 and 10, so each gets an ellipsis.
Page 2 is never added to the set; only the first page, the last page and the current page with its two neighbours are.
Only one neighbour on each side (`current - 1` and `current + 1`) is added, so 6 is not in the set.
The loop pushes an ellipsis whenever two neighbouring numbers differ by more than 1.

explanation: A set of "always show" pages (first, last, current and its siblings), filtered to the valid range, sorted, and joined with an ellipsis wherever there is a gap, is a compact way to build the page bar. Note the edge case the output exposes: here the first `…` hides only page 2, which takes the same space as the number itself. A polished version shows the page instead of an ellipsis when the gap is exactly one page. Interviewers like candidates who spot that.

options.text: Call `setPage(1)` next to `setQuery(...)` in the input's change handler
options.why: Both updates come from the same event, so React batches them into one render that already shows page 1 of the new results.

options.text: Add `useEffect(() => setPage(1), [query])` so the page resets whenever the query changes
options.why: It ends up on page 1, but only after a render that shows the empty page 5. react.dev recommends making the change in the event handler instead.

options.text: Keep `page` in a ref instead of state, so changing the query does not depend on it
options.why: Changing a ref does not re-render, so the page buttons would stop updating, and the stale page number is still used.

options.text: Wrap `setQuery` in `startTransition` so the old page stays on screen until the new results are ready
options.why: A transition changes how urgent the update is, not which page is shown; page 5 is still out of range.

explanation: When one user action should change two pieces of state, change both in the event handler that knows about the action. React batches them, so there is no intermediate render with an impossible combination. Resetting state from an effect that watches another state value causes an extra render with stale data. The same rule applies to sort order and filters: any change that alters the result set should send the user back to page 1.

options.why: It subscribes once on mount and removes the same function on unmount, so no listener leaks.
The cleanup passes a new arrow function. `removeEventListener` only removes the exact function reference that was added, so the listener is never removed.
React only checks dependencies when the component renders. A resize does not cause a render, so this effect never runs again.
Assigning `window.onresize` overwrites any other component's handler, and with no cleanup the handler keeps calling `setWidth` after unmount.

explanation: Subscribing to a browser event is the textbook use of an effect: add the listener in setup and remove the same function in cleanup. Reading `window.innerWidth` in a dependency array does nothing useful, because React only compares dependencies when something else causes a render. Interviewers usually follow up with throttling and server rendering. Note that this version reads `window` in the initializer, which breaks on the server.

options.text: Start with `undefined` (or a fixed default) and read `window.innerWidth` inside the effect, so the server and the first client render match
options.why: Effects do not run on the server, so the window is only read in the browser, after hydration.

options.text: Throttle `onResize` (or schedule it with `requestAnimationFrame`) and cancel any pending call in the cleanup
options.why: This caps how often state updates and re-renders happen during a drag, and the cleanup prevents a late update after unmount.

options.text: Use `typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.innerWidth : 0` in the `useState` initializer
options.why: The server renders 0 and the browser renders the real width, so the first client render does not match the server HTML and causes a hydration mismatch.

options.text: Switch to `useLayoutEffect` so resize events are batched before the browser paints
options.why: `useLayoutEffect` changes when the effect runs, not how often the resize event fires, and it does not run on the server either.

options.text: Listen for `resize` on `document` instead of `window`, which fires less often
options.why: The resize event is fired at the window. A listener on `document` never sees it.

explanation: Browser-only values must not be read during a render that also runs on the server. Render a neutral value first and measure in an effect, or use `useSyncExternalStore` with a `getServerSnapshot`. Resize events fire in bursts, so throttle the state update and cancel it on cleanup. If the component only needs to switch layout at a breakpoint, a CSS media query avoids JavaScript entirely, and interviewers like to hear that.

stem: An OTP input renders 6 single-digit `<input>` boxes with `.map()`. After the user types a digit, focus must move to the next box. Which approach does that correctly?

options.text: One `useRef([])` filled by `ref={el => { inputs.current[i] = el; }}`; the change handler calls `inputs.current[i + 1]?.focus()`
options.why: A ref callback stores every DOM node in one array, and focusing from the event handler happens right after the user types.

options.text: Store the `active` index in state and render `autoFocus={i === active}` on each box
options.why: `autoFocus` only takes effect when an input is mounted. Changing it on an existing input does not move focus.

options.text: Create one `const inputRef = useRef(null)`, pass `ref={inputRef}` to every box, and call `inputRef.current.focus()` after each digit
options.why: One ref object can point at only one node. After rendering it holds the last box, so focus always jumps to the end.

options.text: Call `useRef()` inside the `.map()` callback so each box gets its own ref
options.why: Hooks must not be called inside loops. It breaks the Rules of Hooks, and the hook order changes if the number of boxes ever changes.

explanation: For a list of DOM nodes, keep a single ref that holds an array (or a Map) and fill it with a ref callback. Moving focus is a reaction to a user action, so do it in the event handler, not in an effect that watches state. Interviewers then ask about backspace (move back when the box is empty) and paste (spread the digits across boxes).

stem: The OTP digits live in `const [digits, setDigits] = useState(['', '', '', '', '', ''])`, and `inputs` is an array ref of the boxes. Expected behaviour: Backspace in a filled box clears it as normal, and Backspace in an **empty** box clears the previous box and moves focus there. Which handler does that?

options.why: It only acts when the current box is empty, builds a new array, and moves focus. In a filled box the browser deletes the digit as usual.
When the box is already empty, Backspace changes nothing, so no change event fires and the handler never runs.
This mutates the state array and passes the same reference back. React compares with `Object.is`, sees no change, and skips the re-render.
It also jumps back from a filled box, so the user cannot simply delete the current digit, and the previous box is never cleared.

explanation: Backspace on an empty input produces no change event, so OTP inputs handle it in `onKeyDown`. Update state with a new array (`map`, or spread then assign) so React sees a new reference. `preventDefault` means the handler fully owns this keystroke, so the browser does not also apply Backspace after focus has moved. This is the "classic bug" round of the OTP machine-coding question.

options.why: Non-digits are stripped to `1234567`, boxes 1 to 5 are filled, the extra digits 6 and 7 are dropped, and focus is clamped to the last box.
Filling starts at `start`, which is 1, so the `9` in the first box is kept.
`\D` matches every non-digit, including the space and the hyphen, so they are removed before splitting.
The `start + k < next.length` check stops writes past the last box, so the array keeps its 6 slots, and `Math.min` caps focus at 5.

explanation: A paste handler for split inputs should prevent the default (otherwise the browser puts the whole string into one box), keep only digits, fill from the focused box onwards in a copy of the array, ignore overflow, and move focus to the next empty box or the last one. Copying with `[...digits]` keeps the state update immutable.

stem: An interviewer asks: "What is prop drilling, and when is it actually a problem?" Which two statements would you want to make? (Choose two.)

options.text: It means passing a prop through components that do not use it, only so a deeper component can receive it
options.why: That is the definition: the middle layers become couriers for data they do not care about.

options.text: Context suits values that many distant components read and that change rarely, such as theme, locale or the signed-in user, because every consumer re-renders when the value changes
options.why: This is the trade-off: Context removes the plumbing, but a frequently changing value re-renders all its consumers.

options.text: Drilling is mainly a performance problem, because every extra level a prop passes through adds a re-render
options.why: The cost is maintainability. A parent re-render re-renders its children whether or not a prop is passed through them.

options.text: Passing a prop down two levels is already an anti-pattern that should be replaced with Context
options.why: Explicit props for a couple of levels are clear and easy to trace; react.dev suggests starting with props.

options.text: Redux or a similar store is required once data has to cross more than three components
options.why: Composition or Context often solve it without a library; the number of levels alone does not decide.

explanation: Prop drilling is a code-structure problem: intermediate components gain props they do not use, and renaming or adding data touches every layer. Fix it in this order: first composition (pass the element or `children` down so the middle layers do not need the data), then Context for widely needed values that change rarely, and a store only when shared client state is complex. Interviewers want to hear that Context has a re-render cost, not "just use Context".

options.text: `App` creates `<UserMenu user={user} onLogout={logout} />` and passes it down as a `footer` element that `Sidebar` simply renders
options.why: The element is created where the data lives; the layout components only place it and no longer know about `user`.

options.text: Spread all props at every level with `<Sidebar {...props} />` so the middle components do not name them
options.why: The data still travels through every layer; it is only hidden, which makes it harder to see what each component needs.

options.text: Move the state into a `useUser()` custom hook that wraps `useState`, then call `useUser()` in both `App` and `UserMenu` so they share the user
options.why: Each call to a custom hook gets its own independent state. `UserMenu` would never see the user that `App` sets.

options.text: Move the `user` state down into `UserMenu`, since that is where it is displayed
options.why: `App` and other parts of the tree still need the user (for example for routing), so the state would have to be lifted back up.

explanation: Composition is the first fix react.dev suggests: let the component that owns the data create the element and pass it down as JSX. The middle layers just render `children` or a slot prop. Custom hooks share logic, not state; only Context, a store, or lifting state shares the actual value.

stem: You are migrating a class component to a function component. Which two mappings from lifecycle methods to hooks are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: A subscription made in `componentDidMount` and removed in `componentWillUnmount` becomes one `useEffect` with `[]` that subscribes and returns the unsubscribe function
options.why: Setup and cleanup live together in one effect, which is what the paired class methods did.

options.text: `componentDidUpdate` that refetches when `prevProps.userId !== this.props.userId` becomes `useEffect(() => { ... }, [userId])`
options.why: The effect re-runs when `userId` changes. Unlike `componentDidUpdate`, it also runs on mount, which covers the class component's mount fetch too.

options.text: `shouldComponentUpdate` becomes a `useEffect` that returns `false` to skip the next render
options.why: An effect's return value is a cleanup function; it cannot cancel a render. The closest equivalent is wrapping the component in `memo`.

options.text: `componentWillUnmount` becomes a `useEffect` with no dependency array whose body runs when the component unmounts
options.why: An effect body runs after renders. Unmount logic goes in the cleanup function, and with no dependency array that cleanup also runs before every re-run.

options.text: `componentDidCatch` becomes a `try/catch` around the returned JSX in the function component
options.why: Rendering errors in children are not thrown inside your function, so `try/catch` cannot catch them. Error boundaries still need a class (or a library wrapper).

explanation: Think in terms of synchronisation, not lifecycle events: an effect says "keep this in sync with these values", and its cleanup undoes the previous sync. Mount plus unmount maps to `[]`; did-update for a prop maps to that prop in the dependency array. `shouldComponentUpdate` maps to `memo`, and error boundaries remain the one thing that still needs a class component.

stem: An interviewer asks: "Is `useEffect(fn, [])` exactly the same as `componentDidMount`?" Which answer is accurate for React 19?

options.text: Not exactly: it usually runs after paint (`componentDidMount` runs before paint, like `useLayoutEffect`), and StrictMode in development runs it twice
options.why: Both differences are real: the timing matches `useLayoutEffect` more closely, and StrictMode deliberately double-invokes effects in development.

options.text: Yes: both run exactly once, synchronously, right after React updates the DOM and before the browser paints, in development and in production
options.why: That describes `componentDidMount` and `useLayoutEffect`. A passive effect is usually deferred until after paint.

options.text: No: an empty array means "no restrictions", so the effect runs after every render
options.why: That is what happens with no dependency array at all. `[]` means the effect only runs on mount (plus the StrictMode dev re-run).

options.text: No: the effect runs before the component's DOM is created, so refs are still `null` inside it
options.why: Effects run after commit, so refs to DOM nodes are already attached.

explanation: `useEffect` with `[]` is the usual replacement for `componentDidMount`, but it is not identical. Passive effects are normally flushed after paint, so a measurement that must happen before the user sees the frame belongs in `useLayoutEffect`. In development, StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts once to check that your cleanup undoes the setup. (Reasoned from react.dev's useEffect and useLayoutEffect references.)

options.why: When `url` changes, the cleanup aborts the old request, so its response can never call `setData`. The abort error is expected and ignored.
All requests share one flag. The new effect resets it to `false` right after the cleanup set it to `true`, so the slow old response still gets through.
`await` only orders the steps inside one effect run. Two runs still have two independent requests, and whichever finishes last wins.
React does not know about your requests. Without a cleanup, nothing stops the old response from calling `setData`.

explanation: Responses can arrive out of order, so a fetching effect needs a cleanup that makes the old request harmless: an `ignore` variable local to that effect run, or an `AbortController` that also cancels the network request. The flag has to belong to one effect run; a shared ref is reset by the next run. Interviewers ask this as a follow-up to "write useFetch" to see whether you know about the race.

options.text: Compute `const key = JSON.stringify(options)`, depend on `[url, key]`, and pass `JSON.parse(key)` to `fetch` inside the effect
options.why: An equal options object produces the same string, so the effect only re-runs when the content changes.

options.text: Remove `options` from the dependency array, so only a new `url` triggers a refetch
options.why: The loop stops, but changed headers are ignored and the effect uses stale options; the linter flags the missing dependency.

options.text: Wrap it as `const stable = useMemo(() => options, [options])` inside the hook and list `stable` in the dependency array instead of the raw object
options.why: `options` is a new object each render, so the memo recomputes every time and returns the new object.

options.text: Depend on `[url, options.headers]` instead of the whole options object
options.why: The `headers` object is created inline too, so it is also new on every render.

explanation: Objects and functions created during render are new on each render, so they make poor dependencies. If you cannot ask callers to memoise them, depend on a primitive derived from them (a serialized key, or the specific fields you use). This has caveats: key order matters for `JSON.stringify`, and it does not work for functions or `AbortSignal`s. Data libraries solve this with a serializable `queryKey`.

stem: After you write an effect-driven `useFetch(url)` for GET requests, the interviewer asks you to support submitting a form with POST. What is the right design?

options.text: A separate hook that returns `{ execute, loading, error }`, where `execute(body)` sends the POST and is called from the submit handler
options.why: A POST is caused by a user action, so it belongs in the event handler; the hook only tracks its status.

options.text: Add `method` and `body` parameters to `useFetch`, and include `body` in the effect's dependency array so that each new form body is sent to the server
options.why: The effect would send the POST on mount and again every time the form state changes, and twice in StrictMode development.

options.text: Set a `submitted` flag in the submit handler and have an effect send the POST when the flag becomes `true`
options.why: It works, but routes an event through state and an effect for no reason; react.dev specifically recommends sending such requests from the handler.

options.text: Send the POST inside `useMemo` with `[body]` so it only runs during render when the body changes
options.why: Render must be pure. Side effects in `useMemo` can run more than once or be skipped, and React may discard the render.

explanation: Effects are for synchronising with something because the component is shown (loading data for the current URL). A request that happens because the user clicked Submit is an event, so send it from the event handler. That is why data libraries separate queries (`useQuery`) from mutations (`useMutation`). A mutation hook still returns `loading` and `error` for the UI.

options.text: `a`, `b` and `c`, each about 100 ms after its call
options.why: `id` is declared inside the returned function, so each call clears its own fresh `undefined` id and never cancels an earlier timer.

options.text: Only `c`, about 100 ms after the last call
options.why: That is what a working debounce does, but here no call can reach an earlier call's timer id.

options.text: Only `a`, because later calls are ignored until 100 ms pass
options.why: That describes a leading-edge throttle, and nothing in this code ignores calls.

options.text: Nothing, because each call clears the timer that the previous call set
options.why: Each call only clears its own new, undefined `id`; the earlier timers are left running.

explanation: The timer id must live in the closure shared by every call, which means declaring it next to the returned function, not inside it. A correct debounce: `let id; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(id); id = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); }`. Interviewers often ask for this first and then add `cancel`, `flush` or a leading-edge option. Verified by running in Node.

options.text: `fn` runs once, about 300 ms after the last call, with `this` set to `editor` and the argument `2`
options.why: The second call cancels the first timer. The arrow function inside `setTimeout` keeps the `this` of the wrapper call, which is `editor`.

options.text: Writing the returned wrapper as an arrow function would break `this` when the debounced function is used as a method
options.why: An arrow function takes `this` from where it was defined (inside `debounce`), not from `editor.save(...)`.

options.text: Calling `clearTimeout(id)` on the first call throws, because `id` is still `undefined`
options.why: `clearTimeout` ignores ids that do not match a timer, including `undefined`.

options.text: While calls keep coming, `fn` still runs once every 300 ms
options.why: That is throttle. A debounce keeps postponing until the calls pause for 300 ms.

options.text: `fn` is called with the arguments of the first call, because they were captured first
options.why: Each call schedules a new timer with its own `args`; only the last timer survives, so the last arguments win.

explanation: A complete debounce keeps one timer id in a shared closure, clears it on every call, and forwards both `this` and the latest arguments. A regular `function` wrapper receives the caller's `this`; the inner arrow passes it through to `fn.apply`. Throttle differs because it runs at most once per window while calls continue. Verified by running in Node.

options.text: The returned function stays the same across renders, it always calls the latest `fn`, and a pending call is dropped when the component unmounts
options.why: `useCallback` with `[ms]` keeps it stable, `fnRef` is updated after every render, and the unmount cleanup clears the timer.

options.text: Because the callback is memoised with only `[ms]`, it keeps calling the `fn` from the first render
options.why: The timer calls `fnRef.current`, which the first effect updates after every render, so the latest `fn` is used.

options.text: The unmount cleanup only clears the first timer, because it captured `timer.current` when the component mounted
options.why: The cleanup reads `timer.current` when it runs, so it clears whichever timer is pending at unmount.

options.text: It does not debounce, because `useCallback` returns a new function on every keystroke and each new function keeps its own separate timer in its closure
options.why: The timer lives in a ref shared by all renders, and the callback is only recreated when `ms` changes.

explanation: In React, the debouncer must survive re-renders, or each render gets a new timer and nothing is coalesced. Keep the timer in a ref, return a stable callback, read the latest handler from a ref so it is never stale, and clear the timer on unmount so a late call does not run against an unmounted screen. Reasoned from react.dev's guidance on refs and effects; the timer logic was run in Node.

options.text: `before`, `reducer inc`, `subscriber 1`, `after 1`
options.why: `dispatch` is synchronous: it runs the reducer, stores the result and notifies subscribers before returning.

options.text: `before`, `after 0`, `reducer inc`, `subscriber 1`
options.why: Plain Redux dispatch is not asynchronous; the state has changed by the time the next line runs.

options.text: `before`, `reducer inc`, `after 1`, then `subscriber 1` on a later tick
options.why: Subscribers are called inside `dispatch`, before it returns, not on a later tick.

options.text: `before`, `subscriber 0`, `reducer inc`, `after 1`
options.why: Subscribers are notified after the reducer has produced the new state, never before.

explanation: Redux data flow in one line: the UI dispatches an action, the store calls the root reducer with the current state and the action, saves the returned state, and notifies every subscriber, all synchronously. React-Redux is one of those subscribers: it re-runs selectors and re-renders components whose selected value changed. Async work happens in middleware such as thunks, before an action reaches the reducer. Verified with a minimal store in Node that follows the documented dispatch steps.

options.text: The reducer mutates and returns the same objects, so `useSelector` sees the same `items` reference and skips the re-render
options.why: `useSelector` compares the old and new selected values with `===`. The pushed array is still the same array.

options.text: Redux freezes the state, so `push` throws and the action is silently dropped
options.why: Plain Redux does not freeze state; the push succeeds and the data really is in the array.

options.text: Reducers run asynchronously, so the component reads the state before the push has happened
options.why: Reducers run synchronously during `dispatch`.

options.text: `useSelector` only re-renders when the root state object changes, and a reducer written as a `switch` statement can never replace the root object
options.why: Returning `state` from a switch is fine; the problem is that nothing returned is a new object.

explanation: Reducers must be pure and must not mutate: return new objects for everything that changed, for example `return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] }`. Redux and React-Redux detect changes by reference, so mutation makes updates invisible and breaks time-travel debugging. Redux Toolkit lets you write `state.items.push(...)` only because Immer turns it into an immutable update. Verified in Node that the mutated store keeps the same `items` reference.

options.text: It runs at double speed after the second Start, and after Pause it keeps running at normal speed
options.why: The second Start overwrites the ref, so the first interval's id is lost. Pause clears only the second interval.

options.text: The second Start replaces the first interval, so the stopwatch runs at normal speed and Pause stops it as expected
options.why: Assigning a new id to the ref does not clear the old interval; both keep running.

options.text: It runs at double speed, and Pause stops both intervals
options.why: `clearInterval` takes one id, and only the latest id is in the ref.

options.text: The functional update `m => m + 10` merges the two intervals into one
options.why: The updater avoids stale values, but each interval still adds 10 on every tick.

explanation: Guard Start: return early if `idRef.current` is already set (or clear it first), and set the ref back to `null` in Pause and Reset. Also clear the interval in an unmount cleanup. This is the most common bug in the stopwatch machine-coding round. Verified in Node with real timers: after Pause the counter kept increasing.

stem: A countdown adds 1 second to `elapsed` every time `setInterval(..., 1000)` fires. After the tab has been in the background for a minute, it shows far less time passed than really has. Which design stays accurate?

options.text: Store `startedAt = Date.now()` when started (plus time already accumulated), and on each tick compute `elapsed = accumulated + Date.now() - startedAt`
options.why: The interval only triggers a re-render; the time comes from the clock, so late or skipped ticks do not matter.

options.text: Use a 100 ms interval and add 100 ms per tick, so missed ticks cost less
options.why: Background tabs throttle short timers too, so the count still falls behind, just in smaller steps.

options.text: Replace `setInterval` with a recursive `setTimeout` so each tick waits for the previous one
options.why: It still assumes each tick took exactly the delay, and throttled timers still fire late.

options.text: Count `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks and multiply by 16.67 ms
options.why: Frame rates vary, and browsers pause animation frames in background tabs, so the count stops.

explanation: Timers only promise a minimum delay. Browsers throttle them in background tabs, and a busy main thread delays them too. So never treat the number of ticks as the time. Derive elapsed time from timestamps (`Date.now()` or `performance.now()`) and use the interval only to refresh the display. Pause stores the accumulated time; Resume sets a new `startedAt`.

options.why: Minutes are total minutes (62) rather than minutes within the hour; `padStart` pads 1 and 5 to two digits.

options.text: `01:02:05`, because `Math.floor` already keeps the minutes below 60
options.why: `Math.floor` only rounds down; 3725 / 60 floors to 62. Getting 02 needs `Math.floor(totalSeconds / 60) % 60`, which this code does not do.
`padStart(2, '0')` adds the leading zeros to the one-digit values.
3725 seconds is 62 minutes and 5 seconds; nothing here subtracts a full hour from 62 and gets 1.

explanation: 3725 seconds is 1 hour, 2 minutes and 5 seconds. The minutes must be taken modulo 60: `Math.floor(totalSeconds / 60) % 60`. `String(n).padStart(2, '0')` gives the two-digit fields. Interviewers use this small formatting step to see whether you test edge cases such as values past one hour. Verified by running in Node.

options.text: `0.83`: the USD effect sets 0.01, which makes the INR effect overwrite the typed value
options.why: 1 / 83.17 rounds to 0.01; 0.01 × 83.17 rounds to 0.83; then 0.83 / 83.17 rounds to 0.01 again, so the loop stops with INR at 0.83.

options.text: `1`: each effect only runs when its own field is edited
options.why: Effects run when their dependency changes for any reason, including another effect's `setUsd`.

options.text: It loops forever: each effect keeps triggering the other, and React throws "Maximum update depth exceeded"
options.why: After two round trips the values stop changing, so React bails out of the identical update and the loop ends.

options.text: `0`: the USD effect runs first on mount and resets INR to 0
options.why: The mount effects ran when both were 0; typing changes only `inr`, so only the INR effect runs next.

explanation: Two pieces of state that are kept in sync with effects fight each other: every sync is an extra render, and lossy steps such as rounding change the value the user typed. Store only what the user typed (and which field it was) and compute the other field during render, or update both in the change handler. This bug is what interviewers look for in the interdependent-fields round. Effect sequence reasoned from react.dev and simulated in Node.

stem: You are building a Celsius/Fahrenheit converter where the user can type in either box and the other box updates. Which two designs avoid sync bugs? (Choose two.)

options.text: Store `{ value, scale }` for the box the user last typed in, and compute the other box during render
options.why: There is one source of truth; the typed box shows exactly what was typed and the other is always derived from it.

options.text: In each box's `onChange`, set that box's value and the converted value of the other box together
options.why: Both updates come from one event and are batched into one render, with no effect chain.

options.text: Keep both values in state and add two effects, each updating the other box when its own value changes
options.why: Effects chain extra renders, and a lossy conversion can overwrite what the user typed.

options.text: Use the same two syncing effects but switch them to `useLayoutEffect` so the user never sees the intermediate value
options.why: It hides the flicker but keeps the ping-pong and the overwritten input.

options.text: Keep both values in refs and read them in render, so changing one does not trigger a loop
options.why: Changing a ref does not re-render, so neither box would update on screen.

explanation: When values depend on each other, keep the minimal state (what the user entered) and derive the rest during render. React's own temperature example lifts `{ value, scale }` to the parent for exactly this reason. If you need several stored values, update them together in the event handler. Remember the edge cases: an empty or invalid input should leave the other box empty rather than showing `NaN`.

stem: A sign-up form shows "Invalid email" as soon as the user types the first letter of their email. The requirement: show a field's error only after the user has left that field, or after they press Submit. Which approach meets it?

options.text: Derive `errors` from `values` during render, set `touched[name] = true` in `onBlur`, set `submitted` on submit, and show an error when `(touched[name] || submitted) && errors[name]`
options.why: Errors are always up to date, and the touched/submitted flags only control when each one is shown.

options.text: Compute errors in a `useEffect` that watches `values` and copies them into an `errors` state
options.why: The errors still appear while typing, and the effect adds an extra render with stale errors in between.

options.text: Validate only in `onSubmit`, and clear all errors whenever any field changes
options.why: Nothing appears when the user leaves a bad field, and fixing one field hides the errors of the others.

options.text: Show the error only when the field's value is not empty
options.why: A non-empty but unfinished value is exactly what the user has while typing, so the error still shows too early.

explanation: Separate "is it valid?" from "should we show it yet?". Validity can be derived from the values on every render. Visibility depends on interaction state: `touched` (set on blur) and `submitted`. This is what form libraries track for you (React Hook Form's `mode: 'onTouched'`, Formik's `touched`).

stem: The email field has an error. Which markup makes the error available to screen-reader users when the input is focused?

options.text:
```jsx

Enter a valid email

```
options.why: `aria-invalid` marks the field as invalid, and `aria-describedby` links the error text so it is read with the field.

options.text:
```jsx {/* the message sits right under the field, in red */}

Enter a valid email

```
options.why: Colour and position are visual only; nothing connects the message to the input for assistive technology.

options.text:
```jsx
<label htmlFor={id}>Email</label>
<input id={id} title="Enter a valid email" />
```
options.why: `title` is a tooltip that is announced inconsistently and is not shown on touch devices, so many users never get the error.

options.text:
```jsx
<input id={id} placeholder="Enter a valid email" />
```
options.why: There is no label, and a placeholder disappears as soon as the user types, so it cannot hold an error.

explanation: An accessible error has a programmatic link to its field: give the message an id, point `aria-describedby` at it, and set `aria-invalid`. Generate ids with `useId` so they stay unique and match between server and client. For errors shown after submit, also move focus to the first invalid field or to an error summary. Rendered with `react-dom/server`: React outputs `aria-invalid="true"` and the matching `aria-describedby`.

stem: An interviewer asks how you would handle validation for a checkout form, and whether you would use controlled inputs or React Hook Form. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Client-side validation is for user experience; the server must validate the same rules again, because requests can be sent without the form
options.why: Anyone can call the API directly or change the page's JavaScript, so only server checks are trusted.

options.text: For a small form (a few fields), controlled inputs with `useState` are fine; a re-render per keystroke of a small form is cheap
options.why: Reach for a form library when the form is large, dynamic or slow, not by default.

options.text: React Hook Form requires every input to be controlled through `value` and `onChange`
options.why: Its `register` API uses uncontrolled inputs and reads values from the DOM; `Controller` exists for components that must be controlled.

options.text: Native constraint attributes such as `required` and `type="email"` cannot be used in React forms
options.why: They work in React and give built-in validation and correct mobile keyboards.

options.text: Validation has to run in a `useEffect` after each change so that the error state stays in sync
options.why: Errors can be derived during render or computed in the handler; an effect only adds a render with stale errors.

explanation: A good answer covers three points: where validation runs (client for UX, server for trust), when errors show (on blur or submit, not on every keystroke), and the tool choice. Controlled state is simple and fine for small forms. React Hook Form keeps inputs uncontrolled for large forms. Schema libraries (Zod, Yup) let you share rules between client and server.

stem: With React Router, signed-out users who open `/settings` must go to `/login`, and after signing in they must land back on `/settings`. Which guard does that?

options.why: It redirects during render without showing the page, remembers where the user was going, and `replace` keeps the login redirect out of the history stack.
It calls `navigate` during render (a side effect React Router warns about), still renders the protected children, and forgets the return location.
The protected page renders first and its effects (such as API calls) run before the redirect, and the return location is lost.
A full page load throws away the app's in-memory state, and it still renders the children while the browser navigates.

explanation: A route guard decides what to render: either the protected content or a `<Navigate>` element. Passing the current location in `state` lets the login page send the user back afterwards, and `replace` keeps the Back button from bouncing to the guard. While the auth state is still loading, render a spinner rather than redirecting. Reasoned from the React Router documentation for `Navigate` and `useLocation`.

stem: An app shows admin pages only to users whose role is `admin`. Which two statements about this role-based access control are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Route guards only change what the UI shows; every API endpoint must check the caller's role on the server
options.why: Anyone can call the API directly with their own token, so the server is the only place where a check is enforced.

options.text: Authentication establishes who the user is; authorisation decides what that user may do
options.why: A signed-in viewer is authenticated but is not authorised to delete users.

options.text: Keeping the role in `localStorage` is safe, because users cannot edit it
options.why: Anyone can edit `localStorage` in DevTools; at most this changes their own UI.

options.text: Lazy-loading the admin pages makes them secure, because the code is only downloaded for admins
options.why: The chunk is a public file that anyone can request; code splitting is a performance tool, not access control.

options.text: A JWT's payload is encrypted, so the browser cannot read the role inside it
options.why: A standard signed JWT is only base64url-encoded; anyone can decode it. The signature stops tampering, not reading.

explanation: In a single-page app, a protected route is a user-experience feature: it hides screens that the user cannot use. Security lives on the server, which checks identity and permissions on every request. Interviewers ask this to see whether you separate authentication from authorisation and whether you understand that anything shipped to the browser can be read and changed.

stem: Where should a React app keep its long-lived session or refresh token, and why?

options.text: In an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie: page scripts cannot read it, so an XSS bug cannot steal it, but you still need CSRF protection and XSS can still act as the user while the page is open
options.why: This limits what an XSS attack can take away, while acknowledging the cookie trade-offs.

options.text: In `localStorage`, because cookies are sent automatically and so every cookie is open to CSRF
options.why: Any script running on the page, including injected ones, can read `localStorage` and send the token anywhere. `SameSite` and CSRF tokens handle CSRF.

options.text: In `sessionStorage`, because it is scoped to one tab and so scripts cannot read it
options.why: Scripts on the same page can read `sessionStorage` just like `localStorage`; it only expires sooner.

options.text: In `localStorage`, encrypted with a key stored in the JavaScript bundle
options.why: The key ships to every browser, so an attacker's script can decrypt the token as easily as your code can.

explanation: The usual answer: keep the long-lived token in an `HttpOnly` cookie that JavaScript cannot read, protect it against CSRF with `SameSite` and, where needed, an anti-CSRF token, and keep short-lived access tokens in memory if the API needs a header. Then explain the remaining risk: XSS cannot steal an `HttpOnly` cookie, but it can still send requests while the page is open, so preventing XSS still matters.

stem:
Clicking anywhere inside this modal, even in the input, closes it. It should only close when the user clicks the dark backdrop. Which two changes fix it? (Choose two.) ```jsx
```

options.text: On the backdrop, use `onClick={e => { if (e.target === e.currentTarget) onClose(); }}`
options.why: `target` is the element that was clicked and `currentTarget` is the backdrop, so they match only for clicks on the backdrop itself.

options.text: Add `onClick={e => e.stopPropagation()}` to the inner dialog `div`
options.why: Clicks inside the dialog no longer bubble to the backdrop. It works, but it also hides those clicks from any outer listeners.

options.text: Add `onClick={e => e.preventDefault()}` to the inner dialog `div`
options.why: `preventDefault` cancels the browser's default action; it does not stop the event from bubbling to the backdrop.

options.text: On the backdrop, use `onClick={e => { if (e.currentTarget.classList.contains('backdrop')) onClose(); }}`
options.why: `currentTarget` is always the element the handler is on, which is the backdrop, so this still closes on every click.

options.text: Move `onClick={onClose}` from the backdrop to the inner dialog `div`
options.why: Then clicks inside the dialog close it, and clicks on the backdrop do nothing.

explanation: Click events bubble from the clicked element up through its ancestors, so the backdrop handler sees clicks from inside the dialog. Compare `e.target` with `e.currentTarget`, or stop propagation at the dialog. A further edge case interviewers like: if a user starts a text selection inside the dialog and releases on the backdrop, the click fires on the backdrop. Robust modals also check where `mousedown` started.

options.text: Define `const onKey = e => { ... }` inside the effect, add it, and return `() => document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey)`
options.why: Every listener that is added is removed with the same function reference when the modal closes or `onClose` changes.

options.text: Return `() => document.removeEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'Escape') onClose(); })`
options.why: A new arrow function is a different reference, so `removeEventListener` removes nothing.

options.text: Remove `onClose` from the dependency array, so the effect re-runs only when `open` changes and the listener is added only once per opening
options.why: Listeners still pile up on every open, and the handler would call a stale `onClose`.

options.text: Switch to `useLayoutEffect` so the listener is attached before the modal paints
options.why: The timing is not the problem; without a cleanup the listeners are never removed.

explanation: Every subscription made in an effect needs a cleanup that undoes it, using the same function reference. Here each opening (and each new `onClose` from the parent) adds another listener that is never removed. A complete modal also traps focus, returns focus to the trigger when it closes, and is labelled with `aria-labelledby`. The native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()` gives you Escape handling and inert background content for free.

stem: You are building an infinite-scroll feed that loads the next page when the user nears the bottom. `loadMore` is a stable function that sets a `loading` flag while it fetches. Which implementation is correct?

options.text: Render an empty sentinel `<div ref={sentinelRef} />` after the last item, and in an effect create an `IntersectionObserver` (with a `rootMargin` such as `'300px'`) that calls `loadMore()` when `entry.isIntersecting && hasMore && !loading`; observe the sentinel and return `() => observer.disconnect()`
options.why: The browser reports when the sentinel approaches the viewport, the guard stops repeat or useless requests, and the cleanup removes the observer.

options.text: Add a `scroll` listener on `window` that calls `loadMore()` whenever `document.body.scrollHeight - (scrollY + innerHeight) < 300`
options.why: Scroll fires many times while the user is near the bottom. Without a loading guard or throttling it sends duplicate requests, and nothing removes the listener.

options.text: In the effect, create the observer and observe the sentinel, but skip the cleanup, since the sentinel stays mounted
options.why: Each time the effect re-runs (for example when `loading` or `hasMore` changes) another observer is added, so one intersection triggers several loads.

options.text: During render, check `sentinelRef.current.getBoundingClientRect().top < innerHeight` and call `loadMore()` if it is true
options.why: Render must be pure. On the first render the ref is still `null`, and starting a fetch during render can run it several times.

explanation: The standard approach observes a sentinel element placed after the list. `IntersectionObserver` is asynchronous and avoids reading layout on every scroll event. Use `rootMargin` to start loading before the user reaches the end. Guard against requests while one is in flight or when there is nothing left to load, and disconnect the observer in the effect cleanup. Reasoned from react.dev's effect lifecycle and MDN's IntersectionObserver docs.

stem: Your infinite-scroll feed sometimes requests the same page twice: the observer fires again before React has re-rendered with `loading = true`. When the API runs out of pages, it also keeps requesting an empty page. Which two changes fix these problems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep an in-flight flag in a ref: return early if it is set, set it before the request, and clear it in `finally`
options.why: A ref changes immediately, so a second callback in the same moment sees it, unlike state, which updates on the next render.

options.text: Track `hasMore` from the API response, and stop observing (or stop rendering the sentinel) when it is `false`
options.why: With no sentinel in view, the observer has nothing to report, so no requests for empty pages.

options.text: Call `setLoading(true)` first in the callback, because state updates apply immediately
options.why: State updates are applied on the next render; a callback that runs before that still sees `loading` as `false`.

options.text: Set `rootMargin: '0px'` so the observer can only fire once per page
options.why: The margin only changes when the sentinel counts as visible. It can still fire again whenever it re-enters.

options.text: Set `threshold: 1` so the callback runs only once
options.why: The threshold sets how much of the target must be visible; the callback still runs every time that is crossed.

explanation: Duplicate requests come from relying on state as a lock: `setLoading(true)` only takes effect on the next render, so a second intersection in the meantime still sees `false`. A ref is a synchronous lock. Stopping at the end of the data needs an explicit `hasMore` (or `nextCursor`) from the API. In development, StrictMode also mounts effects twice, so make page appends idempotent (for example by de-duplicating on id). The lock logic was simulated in Node.

options.text: Page 2, then page 2 again, then page 2 again
options.why: The observer callback was created on the first render and always reads `page` as 1, so it always asks for page 2.

options.text: Page 2, then page 3, then page 4
options.why: That would need the callback to read the latest `page`, but the effect with `[]` never re-creates it.

options.text: Only page 2, because the effect runs only once
options.why: The effect runs once, but the observer it creates keeps firing on every intersection.

options.text: Page 2 three times at once, because the observer fires for every item on the page
options.why: Only the sentinel is observed, and each request here happens after the previous page has loaded.

explanation: A long-lived callback created in an effect with `[]` captures the state from the first render. Fix it by keeping the page in a ref (`pageRef.current`), by deriving the next page from a cursor that the fetch returns, or by adding `page` to the dependencies so the observer is re-created (with cleanup) after each page. Note that `setPage(p => p + 1)` alone does not fix the request, because `fetchPage(page + 1)` still reads the stale value. The closure behaviour was simulated in Node.
